lead: SM-130686 is an experimental, orally active, non-peptide growth hormone secretagogue built on an oxindole scaffold. It was characterised in the early 2000s as a ghrelin receptor agonist that stimulates growth hormone release [1][2][3]. Compounds of this class are of interest in body-composition discussions because growth hormone and IGF-1 signalling are associated with lean mass and fat metabolism, which is the chain through which a secretagogue could affect physique.

In animal work, repeated oral administration to rats increased body weight and fat-free mass over nine days, and a follow-up analogue was reported to produce body-weight gain in rats [4][6]. These findings come from laboratory studies. SM-130686 is not an approved medicine, and no human efficacy trials have been published; published work consists of medicinal chemistry, laboratory pharmacology, animal studies and analytical methods for doping control [1][4][7].

Pharmacologically it is structurally distinct from earlier growth hormone secretagogues such as MK-677, NN703 and hexarelin [4]. Its authors describe the oxindole series as emerging from an internal chemical library screen for ghrelin receptor agonists [2].

angle.text: The compound's draw for physique-focused readers is that it is an orally active growth hormone secretagogue, a class associated with higher growth hormone and IGF-1. Evidence for body-composition effects is limited to rat studies; no human data exist.

EC50 about 3.0 nM in rat pituitary cells [1]

paras: The ghrelin receptor was characterised in 1999 as the target of the synthetic growth hormone secretagogues, and in December 1999 Kojima, Kangawa and colleagues described ghrelin, a stomach-derived acylated peptide, as its natural ligand; the name refers to its growth-hormone-releasing role.[10] Ghrelin is also called the hunger hormone because blood levels peak before meals and the peptide stimulates appetite-related neurons in the hypothalamus.[10] Synthetic ghrelin mimetics have been reported to increase body weight and fat mass in animal studies, which is why they are discussed in the context of body composition.[10]

SM-130686 belongs to the non-peptide, orally active branch of this family. Its best-known relative is ibutamoren (MK-677), first described as the oral secretagogue L-163,191 in 1995.[11] Human studies of ibutamoren, which are separate from work on SM-130686, have reported rises in growth hormone and IGF-1 and increases in lean body mass without a change in total or visceral fat.[11] Nothing equivalent has been published for SM-130686.

The active form is the (+)-enantiomer, described as (+)-6-carbamoyl-3-(2-chlorophenyl)-(2-diethylaminoethyl)-4-trifluoromethyloxindole, labelled 37S in the discovery paper; the other enantiomer (37R) showed reduced activity, and the absolute configuration was confirmed by X-ray crystallography [1]. The compound was identified from an internal chemical library as a ghrelin receptor agonist [2]. A 2009 chemistry paper reported a catalytic enantioselective synthesis route [5].

Follow-up structure-activity work substituted the aryl group at the 3-position and produced analogues with subnanomolar binding affinity; one analogue (compound 4i, IC50 0.02 nM) was orally active and gave significant body weight gain in rats over four days [6].

Growth hormone is released in pulses from the pituitary under the control of hypothalamic hormones. Chemically synthesised growth hormone secretagogues were found from the 1970s onward to stimulate and amplify this release, and one of them led to the discovery of the ghrelin receptor and then of ghrelin itself as its endogenous ligand [2]. Wikipedia describes the ghrelin receptor as a G protein-coupled receptor expressed in the hypothalamus, pituitary, liver, skeletal muscle and heart, regulating energy balance and body weight; it lists SM-130686 among its selective agonists [8].

In cultured rat pituitary cells SM-130686 stimulated growth hormone release in a dose-dependent manner (half-maximum at about 6.3 nM), the effect was blocked by a growth hormone secretagogue antagonist but not by a GHRH antagonist, and it displaced a radiolabelled MK-677 ligand from the human receptor (IC50 1.2 nM), indicating that it acts through the ghrelin receptor [4]. In anaesthetised rats a single oral administration raised plasma GH within the first hour, and repeated oral administration over nine days significantly increased body weight and fat-free mass [4]. The compound binds specifically to the receptor and raises intracellular calcium in cells expressing it [2].

Receptor-mapping work with receptor mutants found that SM-130686 and five other agonists, including ghrelin, GHRP-6 and MK-677, shared overlapping binding sites and were all affected by the same key residues [3]. Wikipedia notes that growth hormone secretagogues can also raise IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol [9].

sections.h: Use in appearance and bodybuilding contexts
paras: Growth hormone secretagogues are discussed in physique circles as a route to higher growth hormone and IGF-1 without injecting growth hormone, and some bodybuilders have experimented with ibutamoren.[11] SM-130686 itself is a laboratory compound identified by its research code, and the published literature on it consists of medicinal chemistry and rodent pharmacology.[1][4][6] Its appearance-related interest is therefore a chain drawn from class pharmacology: ghrelin receptor activation, then growth hormone release, then possible changes in fat-free mass, a chain that the rat work above supports only in animals.[4]

The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits growth-promoting agents and secretagogue compounds in sport. A 2006 study developed mass-spectrometry methods for urine screening of growth hormone secretagogue-active drugs, including a structural analogue of SM-130686, as a preventive anti-doping strategy [7].
No studies found. Published work on SM-130686 is limited to chemistry, cell-based assays, animal research and analytical methods [1][4][6][7].

timeline.event: The related oral secretagogue MK-677 (L-163,191) is first described.[11]
Ghrelin is reported as the natural ligand of the growth hormone secretagogue receptor.[10]
Oxindole growth hormone secretagogues, including SM-130686, reported in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry and the Journal of Endocrinology [1][4].
Structure-activity work on the oxindole series reports analogues with subnanomolar affinity [6].
Review of its synthesis and pharmacology; doping-control urine method for secretagogues published [2][7].
Catalytic enantioselective synthesis published; ghrelin receptor binding-site mapping published [3][5].

name: SM-130686

card.summary: An experimental oral oxindole growth hormone secretagogue known from lab and animal papers, with no human trials of muscle or appearance effects.
card.note: Not an approved medicine; no human efficacy or safety trials were found.

quick.overview:
SM-130686 is a research compound that stimulates growth hormone release by activating the ghrelin receptor. Unlike peptide secretagogues it is a small molecule designed to work by mouth.

The literature is mostly chemistry and animal or cell-based pharmacology from the 2000s. No human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It binds and activates the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor, which triggers growth hormone release from pituitary cells in laboratory studies.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been published. The compound is experimental, and analytical methods exist for detecting secretagogues in urine for doping control.
